_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03), passe de correction : chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: In the epic of Sundiata, the name is that of the kings of the land of Do, where Sogolon, Sundiata's mother, comes from: Do Mansa Gnèmo Diarra reigns when the buffalo ravages the country, and the king of Do who comes to fight at the side of his nephew Sundiata is called both Faony Kondé and Faony Diarra. The narrative thus gives one and the same king both names, Kondé and Diarra.
oralTraditions.carrier: Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté, griot de Djeliba Koro, près de Siguiri
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui l'a traduit en français

oralTraditions.claim: A praise song of the land of Do names Mansa Oumalé Kondé and Marfadou Diara together, in the refrain "Do ni Kri". The editor of the epic, who quotes it, places the land of Do in the present-day region of Ségou, presenting this as a hypothesis.
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, dans les notes de l'épopée
oralTraditions.context: Praise song quoted in Maninka with its translation, in a note of the 1960 edition

oralTraditions.claim: The Diarra are said to come from the land of Do, made up of twelve villages whose exact location is not known. Some Diarra are said to descend from the kings of Ségou, and the Kamissoko, their joking partners, are said to be their younger brothers.
oralTraditions.carrier: Des griots que Molinie ne nomme pas
oralTraditions.collector: Molinie, officier de la marine française, en 1959
oralTraditions.context: Account taken from a dictionary written for Europeans posted in French West Africa, cited at second hand in a 2017 thesis that warns against its unfounded generalisations

linguisticReconstructions.claim: The clan name Jàra, of which Diarra is the usual French transcription, is identical to the Bambara word jàra, which means the lion (wáraba is its synonym) and, in a second sense that the dictionary gives separately, the fetish. The epic calls Sundiata "Manding-Diara, lion of the Manding". The dictionary of clan names lists the lion, under both its names, among the clan's prohibitions. No source consulted says whether the clan takes its name from the beast, from the fetish or from something else: the origin of the name is not established.

The lion has long been the object of cults in the West African savannah: the Guinean writer Camara Laye describes his initiation as a child, in northern Guinea, by a lion mask named Konden Diarra, a sign that these cults were still alive at least in the second quarter of the twentieth century. A historian finds it plausible that the name Sundiata, which contains the word jata or jara, draws on them; he derives no explanation of the clan name from it.

Another explanation derives the name from a place name, that of a former political entity, the region of Jara. A 2017 study judges it probable and links two early accounts to this region: a Portuguese text written no later than about 1510, which says that the king of the Mandingas lives in a town surrounded by an earthen wall called Jaga, and the Timbuktu chronicle attributed to Mahmud Kati, which devotes a chapter to a region of Jara subject to the Songhai. The explanation is not established.

The dictionary of clan names reports a prohibition specific to the clan: a Jàra must not look at a newborn child during the first eight days after its birth, or the child would die. No independent source corroborates this note.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: A 2017 study gives the name the status hɔ́rɔn, of free condition, based on survey materials with no named informant; the dictionary of clan names carries no status for the entry Jàra. Some Diarra are said to descend from the kings of Ségou, and a UNESCO synthesis reports that the Diarra of the family of King Ngolo Diarra could not erase the memory of their ancestor's servile status, which the kings of Kaarta mocked.

sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the fiche of the Bambara people.

sources.title: Beyond the Mali Empire — A New Paradigm for the Sunjata Epic
sources.notes: Jansen, Jan, Universiteit Leiden; article published in The International Journal of African Historical Studies, cited from the author's version deposited at Leiden and its pagination. The author argues that the heroes of the Sundiata epic refer to ritual practices rather than to historical persons. Jata or Jara means "lion", the lion being the object of cults in the savannah, and the lion mask Konden Diarra in Camara Laye's novel L'Enfant noir, a sign that these cults were still practised in the second quarter of the twentieth century (p. 14).

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), identified by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The entry Jàra gives the Bambara and Malinke groups, equivalents among other peoples (Condé, Ndiaye, Koné), the lion under its two names, jàra and wáraba, among the prohibitions, the Tarawele, Denbele, Sanogo, Kone, Kanute, Dunbuya and Bagayogo as joking partners, and a note written in Russian, translated here, on the prohibition concerning newborn children; it carries no status and gives no meaning for the name. Koné appears there both as an equivalent and as a joking partner. The pair with Diabaté is carried by the entry Jɛbatɛ. Joking ties are not always reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is cited from the entry that carries it, which may be that of the other name.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. She states what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for all the descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — applied in varying ways today, she notes — and mutual aid is owed without reserve. Cited for the obligation itself; she does not name the pair of this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside her.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship soothes conflicts is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified; the last page is not.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire bambara-français, lexique
sources.notes: Online version of the electronic Bambara-French dictionary whose appendix of clan names is cited separately. The article jàra is glossed there as "lion, Panthera leo", with wáraba as synonym, then "fetish"; a second article Jàra lists it among clan names. Consulted online on 29 September 2026.

sources.title: Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Présence Africaine, 1960. Transcription of the account of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté of Djeliba Koro (Siguiri); it is a written record of an oral tradition. Pages read in the digitised copy on archive.org (SoundjataOuLepopeeMandingue), close to the printed edition without being identical to it: Sundiata called "Manding-Diara, lion of the Manding" (p. 12); Do Mansa Gnèmo Diarra, king of the land of Do (pp. 21-25); the editor's note on the land of Do, which he places in the present-day region of Ségou, and the praise song that names Kondé and Diara (p. 31, note 4); the king of Do, uncle of Sundiata, called Faony Kondé and Faony Diarra (p. 102).

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., undergraduate thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, read by V. Vydrin. Entry Jàra, pp. 54-56: the French spelling Diara (p. 54) and the form Jata among the Mandinka of Gambia and Senegal (p. 56); the status hɔ́rɔn, with no indication of provenance, of the Diarra descended from the kings of Ségou, and the Kamissoko as joking partners and younger brothers of the Diarra, after Molinie 1959 (p. 55); the explanation by a place name, with a Portuguese account cited from the edition by Fernandes and the chronicle attributed to Mahmud Kati, and the origin in the land of Do, after Molinie 1959 (p. 56). Molinie's account rests, according to the author, on the oral tradition collected from griots (p. 4). The data with no indication of provenance come there, according to the author, from the materials gathered by V. Vydrine and A. Davydov, with no place or informant. Molinie, a naval officer, was compiling a dictionary intended for Europeans posted in French West Africa and relied on griots whom he does not name; the thesis warns against his generalisations. An undergraduate thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the accounts it passes on.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, V : L'Afrique du XVIe au XVIIIe siècle — chapitre 12, Du Niger à la Volta
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. B. A. Ogot, 1999; chapter by M. Izard and J. Ki-Zerbo. Printed pages: the reign of Ngolo Diarra at Ségou (1766-1790) (p. 376); the Diarra of the family of the great king Ngolo Diarra, who could not erase the memory of their ancestor's servile status (p. 405).

gaps.reason: Diarra and Jara are two spellings of the same jamu. The dictionary of jamuw lists Condé, Ndiaye and Koné among the equivalents of the entry Jàra — clan names of other peoples held to be the same, not homonyms. No distinct lineage of origin has been found, but since the etymology of the name itself remains open, a homonymy could not be ruled out on this basis.
